Senses.Explanation: Literally “the tongue” (舌頭), deployed in Chan verdicts as a person's capacity to speak. “The tongue has no bone” (舌頭無骨) answers both “what is the great meaning of the buddha teaching?” and “opening the mouth loses; closing it perishes—how can one speak?” A student says that he no longer doubts “the tongues of the old masters everywhere” (天下老和尚舌頭), and his teacher immediately asks him to state what he understands. In the Linji succession account Huangbo predicts that Linji will “sit across and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven” (坐斷天下人舌頭); the same countable verdict recurs widely without narrating bodily injury. The concrete organ is thus the corpus's recurring word for what is tested, trusted, shortened, or cut off in public speech.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense. The headword has 2,473 hits in 325 allowlisted texts; the speech deployment is independently anchored in lamp, lineage, and case-commentary sources. This is a different referent from the anatomical tongue that is bitten or injured, not a second reading imposed on the same passage.

Occurrences.Kwic: 住後僧問。如何是佛法大意。師曰。舌頭無骨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Continued Lamp encounter gives ‘the tongue has no bone’ as the answer to the great meaning of the buddha teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問開口即失閉口即喪。未審如何說。師曰。舌頭無骨。僧曰。不會。師曰。對牛彈琴。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate master answers the open-mouth/closed-mouth dilemma with ‘the tongue has no bone.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 師當下大悟云。某甲不疑天下老和尚舌頭也。山曰。汝會處作麼生。與我說來看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student says he no longer doubts old masters' tongues; the teacher requires him to state his understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子但將去。已後坐斷天下人舌頭去在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo predicts that Linji will later sit across and cut off everyone's tongue.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊被魔王坐斷舌頭，龍淵路見不平，要與雪屈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old-case commentary applies the same speech-verdict collocation to the Buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，僧出擬問，師曰：不動舌頭道將一句來。僧喝，師曰：猶涉唇吻在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public teaching encounter, the master demands a statement without moving the tongue, explicitly testing the monk's capacity to speak.

Senses.Explanation: The anatomical tongue, a bodily organ that can be bitten. The records say “while eating, bite the tongue” (喫飯咬著舌頭) and “just now, eating melon seeds, [I] bit through the tongue” (適纔吃瓜子，咬破舌頭). These bodily predicates identify a separate referent from the tongue used as the capacity for public speech.
Senses.Note: No special Zen deviation is asserted for this ordinary anatomical sense. Independent bodily witnesses prevent the speech sense from absorbing literal anatomy.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct bodily use: biting the tongue while eating.
A second independent bodily use: biting through the tongue while eating melon seeds.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a verse on an old case
AlternateTargets: to compose verses on old cases
collection of verses on old cases
Senses.Explanation: A verse composed on an old recorded case, also the named genre, collection, and act of composing such verses. The corpus treats it as a category beside “picking up old cases” (拈古): “there is picking up old cases; there are verses on old cases” (有拈古焉有頌古焉). It counts and titles the resulting works, including “Xuedou's hundred verses on old cases” (雪竇頌古百則), and a collected record says that “one hundred verses on old cases formed a book” (頌古百首為成書). A Book of Serenity preface compares the verses of Xuedou and Tiantong to Li Bai and Du Fu in poetry. Verbal records say that monks “present their understanding and compose verses on old cases” (呈見解，作頌古), that a retired master composed one hundred, and that Dahui composed one hundred and ten while living at Yunmen hermitage. The poems, genre headings, collections, and composition constructions all concern the same literary product and event; noun and verb grammar does not create a second lexical thing.
Senses.Note: The headword has 1,075 hits in 264 allowlisted texts. Headings, numbered sets, anthologies, prefaces, and composition predicates establish one concrete Chan literary genre. The former result/act targets were grammatical views of the same verse and could not be distinguished as different referents from the targets alone. Compare picking up old cases (拈古), old cases (古則), public cases (公案), and appraisal-commentary (評唱).

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇頌古百則。叢林學道詮要也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record postface calls Xuedou's hundred verses on old cases an essential guide in the monasteries.

Occurrences.Kwic: 頌古。猶詩壇之李杜。世謂雪竇有翰林之才。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Book of Serenity preface compares the two masters' verses on old cases to Li Bai and Du Fu.
An anthology preface names picking up old cases and verses on old cases as sibling literary categories.
A collected record explicitly says that one hundred verses on old cases formed a book.
Dahui describes monks presenting their understanding and composing verses on old cases.
A biographical record says that the master retired, lived in a hermitage, and composed one hundred verses on old cases.

Occurrences.Kwic: 居雲門庵，作頌古一百一十則。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A preface says that Dahui lived at Yunmen hermitage and composed one hundred and ten verses on old cases.
